That's not really true, as far as I'm aware. Many people who are receiving various forms of welfare are counted as unemployed.

If you are able to work and are looking for work, you're generally counted among the unemployed.

What's true is that if you stop looking for employment for an extended period, you're not counted as unemployed.

If I lose my job, my wife picks up more hours, and I decide to quit sending the kids to daycare and take care of them myself, I'm no longer counted as unemployed.

If I have trouble finding work, and I decide to get a degree in a more employable field, I'm not counted as unemployed.

If I'm 65 but was going to work a few more years, get fired or laid off, and decide to retire instead of get a new job, I'm not counted as unemployed.

Many people who are still counted as unemployed are no longer receiving unemployment benefits, as they run out after several months.

Many forms of welfare require people to actively look for work. My brother had to actively look for work to receive food stamps. He is then counted among the unemployed, as he is looking for work.

One instance where people on a form of welfare aren't counted: disability. The rise in disabled people has resulted in a lower unemployment rate.

So the real issue is whether or not the people are looking for work. Some forms of welfare require it. Others don't.
